newsitem.title: UK: Borrowers from around the globe prepare for EMU.
newsitem.headline: Borrowers from around the globe prepare for EMU.

text.p: Borrowers from Brazil to Japan are making preparations to raise funds as cheaply as possible when Europe's single currency is introduced.
"Everyone is trying to position themselves to be able to borrow in the most cost-efficient manner when the euro comes into being," Paul Hearn, syndicate manager at J.P. Morgan said.

At the start of this year a flurry of so-called parallel bonds were launched in core European currencies. The deals redenominate into the euro, due to be introduced on January 1, 1999 when the third phase of European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) kicks in.
But so far only European sovereigns, the European Investment Bank (EIB) and European borrowers like L-Bank and Siemens have tapped this market.
Hearn at J.P. Morgan said the need to establish benchmarks in the euro sector was not just an issue for European credits.

"Post-1999 all the European governments will be borrowing domestic euro-denominated securities. Everyone else needs to position themselves so they don't borrow at too high a premium to those government bonds," he said.
Recently, Brazil said it had asked banks for proposals to issue parallel bonds, and Japan Finance Corp for Municipal Enterprises (JFM) was said to be considering an issue.

Parallel bonds are deals launched in different European currencies with the same coupon and maturity. Then, when the euro is introduced, these different tranches become fungible into a larger euro Eurobond.
Liquidity should be enhanced because the absolute size of the bond will increase, but also because parallel bonds will be traded relative to euro benchmarks.
Although all debt in currencies joining EMU will be redenominated into euros, most will not do so until the original currencies are abolished in 2002.
Between 1999 and 2002, bonds denominated in French francs, guilders, marks etc will be traded but their underlying government bond markets will disappear.
"One of the big points about these fungible bonds is it enhances liquidity, and investors like that," a syndicate manager at a European bank said.
"One complaint about Eurobonds is they tend to become illiquid. Parallel bonds give an opportunity for liquidity over a longer period of time," he said.
Investors also buy them as a way to trade accross markets, made easier because the bonds have the same coupons and maturity.

"The short-term attraction of parallel bonds for investors is in the run-up to EMU they can be used to trade your views on the core countries," a syndicate manager at a European bank active in the sector said.
Euro-related issues were popular in the first quarter of the year, with over $10 billion equivalent issued in the international bond market, adding up to a 5.4 percent market share.
The pace of future deals will depend on investor views on whether EMU will happen on time, bankers said.
"The mood on EMU was very positive at the start of the year, and this allowed so many parallel bonds to be launched successfully," a trader at U.S. bank said.
"There is more caution now, but if a more positive attitude takes hold again more and more borrowers will realise EMU is for real and try to get into the market."
